title: SYSK Selects: How Magic Mushrooms Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2012 episode "How Magic Mushrooms Work," picked by Josh. The hosts cover the history of psychedelic mushrooms (cave paintings, Mesoamerican use, the Aztec "flesh of the gods," Sami reindeer urine), the 1950s R. Gordon Wasson mushroom trip in Mexico and the Life magazine article coining "magic mushroom," Albert Hofmann isolating psilocybin, Sandoz, and Timothy Leary's role. They explain psilocybin/psilocin chemistry and serotonin action, set and setting, effects and tolerance, look-alike toxic mushrooms and spore prints, common Psilocybe species, the legal status and US/UK/Netherlands/Mexico laws, home cultivation outline, and modern research on OCD, cluster headaches, and personality openness (Johns Hopkins, Griffiths). The episode ends with listener mail from Max about getting a job.

segments.title: Selects intro and psychedelic banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a Selects pick from 2012 and the hosts banter about psychedelia, rock bands with mushroom imagery, Chuck's sniffles, and past psychedelics episodes.

segments.title: Ancient and indigenous mushroom use
segments.summary: The hosts discuss claimed prehistoric mushroom depictions in cave paintings in Algeria and Spain, Aztec 'flesh of the gods,' contemporary Mesoamerican tribes' use, and the Sami people and reindeer urine.

segments.title: R. Gordon Wasson and the origin of 'magic mushroom'
segments.summary: Wasson's 1950s mushroom trip in Mexico, described in his Life magazine article, which gave the term magic mushroom. Albert Hofmann then isolated psilocybin, and Sandoz began producing it.

segments.title: Psilocybin research history and Timothy Leary
segments.summary: Early psychiatric research into psilocybin for obsessive disorders, the later US scheduling and shutdown, and Timothy Leary's role in discrediting psychedelic research and popularizing set and setting.

segments.title: Mushroom effects, chemistry, and tolerance
segments.summary: Psilocybin is converted to psilocin, which acts on serotonin receptors. Effects include nausea, euphoria, dysphoria, depersonalization, distorted time, and tolerance building quickly. LSD and mushrooms are chemically similar.

segments.title: Foraging risks, toxic look-alikes, and spore prints
segments.summary: Foraging dangers from toxic Galerina-like look-alikes, the blue-bruising myth, spore print identification, and the common Psilocybe species Cubensis, semilanceata, and bohemica.

segments.title: Buying, dosing, and drying mushrooms
segments.summary: Street sale by weight, drying effects on potency, flavor problems and workarounds such as chocolate, tea, and capsules, and typical doses and onset times.

segments.title: Home cultivation of psilocybin mushrooms
segments.summary: Overview of the grow process: spores, sterile water, substrate cake of vermiculite and flour, sterilizing in jars, mycelium growth, and fruiting. The hosts note that cultivation is illegal.

segments.title: Legal status of psilocybin worldwide
segments.summary: Psilocybin is Schedule I in the US, with mail-order kits targeted from 2003. The UK and Amsterdam/Netherlands restrictions are described, and Mexico and Native American Church exceptions for other substances are noted.

segments.title: Modern medical research on psilocybin
segments.summary: Johns Hopkins studies on OCD and compulsions, cluster headache relief reports, and the Divinity students study with long-term follow-up showing positive life changes, plus a study on increased openness in older adults.

segments.title: Animal studies and The Bear documentary
segments.summary: Psilocybin dosing risks in research, animal studies on rats, mice and monkeys, and a discussion of a bear eating mushrooms in the documentary The Bear.

segments.title: Listener mail from Max
segments.summary: Max writes that after being laid off, listeners' retweets helped, and he has now been hired for an office job near his home in the San Francisco Bay Area.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to contact them on Twitter, Facebook, or email and point to the HowStuffWorks article for more.
